headline_insight: While approximately half of surveyed clients experienced some reduction in financial stress, over 43% of both male and female clients reported that insurance had no effect on their stress levels, and child wellbeing improvements remained limited to less than a third of households.
paragraphs: The 2026 Insurance Survey reveals that while insurance products offer some relief, they have yet to fully alleviate the financial anxieties of most clients. Specifically, 21.5% of female clients and 23.5% of male clients reported that insurance significantly reduced their financial stress, while an additional 29.8% of females and 31.2% of males saw it somewhat reduced. However, a substantial 47.1% of female and 43.2% of male respondents reported that insurance had no effect on their stress levels. This trend is mirrored among households supporting persons with disabilities (PWD), where 47.8% of PWD-headed households reported no effect on financial stress compared to 45.3% of non-PWD households. Benchmark data is not available for this indicator. The qualitative findings highlight the persistent gaps in coverage that leave clients vulnerable; for instance, a female client in Rwanda remarked, 'I used my pocket money,' while a female client in Tanzania noted, 'Nina bima ya NHIF,' indicating reliance on alternative national schemes. For VisionFund, these findings imply a critical need to refine product design and communication to ensure that insurance benefits are tangible enough to actively reduce daily financial anxiety, particularly for highly vulnerable PWD households.

When coping with shocks, clients continue to rely on secondary financial strategies that can jeopardize their long-term resilience. The survey shows that 6.6% of female and 6.5% of males used their savings to cope, while 6.3% of females and 9.7% of males had to borrow money. Though the proportion of clients selling assets or livestock remained low at 1.6% for females and 3.2% for males, the necessity of borrowing highlights that insurance payouts may not be timely or sufficient. This is illustrated by a female client in Uganda who shared that she 'Used the loan to pay her medical bills,' and a female client in Malawi who explained, 'We also contributed 1000 each to pay for our friend because she was admitted for over a month.' These community and debt-based coping mechanisms suggest that formal insurance is not yet fully replacing informal safety nets. Benchmark data is not available for these coping indicators. To address this, VisionFund should consider integrating emergency credit lines or rapid-payout mechanisms into insurance products to prevent clients from accumulating debt during health crises.

The impact of insurance on child wellbeing also remains constrained, with only 31.9% of female and 32.6% of male clients reporting that child wellbeing improved because of the insurance. Similarly, only 31.4% of PWD households and 32.4% of non-PWD households reported positive changes in child wellbeing, while the vast majority (60.1% of females and 58.2% of males) reported no improvement. Among specific benefits, 15.1% of females and 17.4% of males noted improved access to healthcare treatment and diagnosis for children, but only 5.9% of females and 9.2% of males reported fewer school days missed due to improved health. Benchmark data is not available for these child wellbeing indicators. This gap suggests that current insurance products do not sufficiently cover child-specific health and educational needs. VisionFund has a clear opportunity to design targeted family-centric policies, such as pediatric health riders or educational continuity clauses, to ensure that financial protection directly translates into better developmental outcomes for children.
